The short answer: airflow is the whole decision. Airflow was the most-discussed topic in our entire dataset at 1,585 mentions, and the complaint pattern runs in one direction — reviewers rarely say a dryer is too powerful, they say it is too weak for their hair Review analysis. Underpowered dryers are the most common single reason reviewers describe returning one.

Our pick: the Laifen SE2 at about C$145, which is specifically tuned for buyers whose complaint is that a dryer cannot handle dense hair. If you want the largest review base to judge from, the slopehill Brushless at about C$80 has 6,087 Canadian ratings and rates 4.6★.

And the single most common mistake is reaching for higher heat. That makes it worse, for a reason worth understanding.

What actually matters when drying thick hair

Drying thick hair is a water-removal problem, and the amount of water scales with hair mass.

That reframes what the dryer needs to do. It is not primarily a heater — it is a pump for moving air across a wet surface. More air at a lower temperature removes water faster than more heat does, because heat alone does not move water off the hair; it only raises the temperature of the water that is already there.

This is why high-speed brushless dryers changed the category. They move a much larger volume of air for the same or lower power draw than a conventional element dryer. Our data reflects that: the complaints are about weakness, not about power.

The specific failure of using high heat on dense hair is worth spelling out. Heat applied to thick hair dries and seals the outer layer while the interior stays damp. So you get a dry-feeling surface, heat damage to the cuticle, and you still need more drying time — the worst of both outcomes. Heat and temperature generated 1,093 mentions with 54% negative, and this is the pattern behind them.

Two ergonomic factors matter more for you than for most buyers. Thick hair means longer sessions, so weight matters: 1,318 mentions with 73% positive. And because you are working through sections, control placement matters: usability is the second-largest topic in our data at 1,579 mentions with 39% negative, and reviewers describe buttons they cannot find without looking Review analysis.

What we cannot tell you yet: how many cubic metres per minute any of these dryers actually moves. We have not measured it. Every comparison table row for measured airflow on this site reads “not yet tested” rather than carrying an estimate, and that is deliberate.

What does not matter for thick hair

Three things this category markets hardest for dense hair, and none of them holds up.

1. Peak wattage. Wattage describes power draw, not drying speed. A high-speed brushless dryer can move more air than a 1875W conventional dryer while drawing less. “2000W” in a product title tells you less than it appears to — and our complaint data is about weakness, which wattage does not measure.

2. Ion counts. Ionic as a feature has the best record in our data at 17% negative, but that is a frizz benefit, not a drying-speed one. The count itself has no consistent definition across brands.

3. “Professional” or “salon.” Neither has a regulatory or industry definition in this category. They appear on dryers from C$25 to C$630 in our dataset.

What does matter and gets under-marketed: the low heat setting, the weight, and where the controls sit. All three matter more for long sessions on dense hair than any headline number.

How to dry thick hair without a 30-minute session

The method changes the outcome more than the dryer does.

  1. Remove as much water as possible before switching on. Towel or microfibre blot thoroughly. The first minutes of drying soaking hair are the least efficient of the whole session
  2. Section the hair first. Four to six clips. Dense hair dried in one mass takes far longer than the same hair dried in sections
  3. Start at the roots and scalp, then work out. The scalp area holds the most water and is the slowest to dry
  4. Use maximum airflow but medium heat. This is the core principle — more air, less heat
  5. Keep the dryer moving. Holding it still concentrates heat on the surface while the interior stays damp
  6. Do not seal the surface early with high heat. Once the outer layer dries and tightens, the interior takes even longer
  7. Finish with the cool shot. It sets the result and it is the step most people skip

One expectation to set: thick hair takes longer. That is a property of how much water is in it, not a sign your dryer is broken. The question is whether you are removing that water efficiently — which is airflow and sectioning, not heat.

Why weight matters here specifically. If your session is 20 minutes rather than 8, the difference between a 400 g and a 600 g dryer is the difference between finishing comfortably and setting it down. Weight was the third most-discussed topic in our dataset at 1,318 mentions and 73% positive Review analysis.

Three numbers worth carrying into a purchase decision.

Airflow mentions — the most-discussed topic in our dataset1,585

Underpowered dryers as a stated reason for returnThe most common single reason Review analysis
Usability and controls mentions1,579 (39% negative)

How to read this. The volume of airflow discussion tells you it is the thing buyers care about most. The direction of the complaints tells you what goes wrong: not too much power, but too little. And the heat figure tells you what people try instead — which is the mistake.

The usability number deserves attention too. At 1,579 mentions with 39% negative, controls are the second-largest topic. If you are doing a longer session with product on your hands, being able to change settings without looking matters more than it sounds.

What to avoid with thick hair

  • Reaching for maximum heat. It dries the surface, damages the cuticle, and leaves the interior damp
  • Drying the whole head in one section. Sectioning is the single biggest time saver
  • Buying on wattage. It does not measure what you need
  • A heavy dryer. Long sessions make weight a real factor, not a comfort detail
  • A dryer with buttons you cannot find by touch. Usability is the second-largest topic in our data
  • Ignoring the seller structure. With a median reported failure of 5.5 months, a listing with five competing sellers and a third-party Buy Box is the weakest position to be in

Frequently asked questions

What is the best hair dryer for thick hair? The Laifen SE2 at about C$145 is our pick, because it is specifically tuned for buyers whose complaint is that a dryer is underpowered for dense hair. If you want the largest review base to judge from, the slopehill Brushless at about C$80 has 6,087 Canadian ratings and rates 4.6 stars.

Is higher wattage better for thick hair? Not directly. Wattage describes power draw, not drying speed. A modern high-speed brushless dryer moves more air than a 1875W conventional dryer while drawing less power, which is why airflow is the specification to compare and wattage is not. Airflow was the most-discussed topic in our dataset at 1,585 mentions.

Why does my hair dryer take so long on thick hair? Because drying dense hair is a water-removal problem, and the amount of water is proportional to hair mass. More air at a lower temperature removes it faster than more heat, because heat alone does not move water off the hair. Our data shows reviewers rarely complain a dryer is too powerful — they complain it is too weak.

Should I use high heat to dry thick hair faster? No, and it is the most common mistake. Heat and temperature generated 1,093 mentions in our dataset with 54% of them negative. High heat on dense hair dries the outer layer while the interior stays damp, so you end up heat-damaging the surface and still needing more drying time.

What weight should I look for in a dryer for thick hair? Lighter is better, because thick hair means longer sessions and the dryer is held at arm’s length throughout. Weight was the third most-discussed topic in our dataset at 1,318 mentions and 73% of that discussion was positive, so buyers do notice it. We publish measured weight with the cord as units complete our protocol.

Do I need a diffuser for thick hair? Only if your hair is also curly or wavy. Thick, straight hair dries faster with a concentrator because it focuses the airflow where you aim it. Thick, curly hair needs a diffuser to preserve the pattern — see our curly hair guide for that case.

Our verdict for thick and coarse hair

Buy the Laifen SE2 at about C$145. It is tuned for exactly this problem, it has the strongest sales growth in its range at roughly +89% month over month, and it sits in the price band where complaint rates fall to 9.6% from 30.3%.

Buy the slopehill Brushless at about C$80 if you want the most evidence to judge from — 4.6★ from 6,087 ratings and a 5.7-year history. But accept the weakness: five competing sellers and a third-party Buy Box, which is the worst warranty structure in this comparison.

Buy the Dyson Supersonic Travel at about C$400 only if the service network and universal voltage justify 2.8× the Laifen SE2. It has the largest Dyson review base we cover and the only established Canadian service network here.

And change one habit regardless of what you buy: maximum airflow at medium heat, hair sectioned first. More heat is the most common mistake on dense hair, and our data explains exactly why it backfires. For what actually fails and when, see how long hair dryers actually last.
